# Facilitator guide: Impersonation and phishing workshop

Generated by `build/build.py` from `04-content/slides.json`, `src/content/notes.json` and `src/content/choices.json`. Edit those files and rebuild; do not edit this file by hand.

**Status.** Generic build for a sector-neutral audience. Meranti and all its people and messages are fictional. Customer reporting details, date and venue are unconfirmed and appear as bracketed placeholders. No aesthetic approval, customer verification or live rehearsal is recorded.

**Notes are shown on the presentation screen, not privately.** Menu › Presenter notes opens them as a panel over the current slide, so a projected audience sees them. Print this guide, or open it on a separate device, for private reference.

## Before the day

- Confirm audience size, departments, language, room and projector, date and venue.
- Confirm break arrangements for the date and venue. If a longer break is needed, revise the whole timetable; do not shorten the reporting segment.
- Obtain the organisation’s verified reporting route (button, mailbox, urgent phone, steps) and support/ticket process. Enter them in `config/customer-config.json` with `"verified": true` and rebuild. Until then SL70 shows a labelled demo.
- Rehearse locally: open `dist/workshop.html` from disk, test fullscreen (F), the menu (M) with its slide index, presenter notes and sources, and the long reveal states.
- Print the participant response card (`dist/participant-quick-reference.html`) and this guide.
- No learner laptops are required. Use show of hands and table discussion for decisions.

## Module goals and habits

- **Module 1: The borrowed identity**: Anyone can copy a name, photo and job title, and messages that borrow a familiar identity get trusted. You will be able to: Tell a copied profile from a genuine account someone else controls; Spot when a friendly conversation turns into a sensitive request; Respond if someone uses your name.
    - Habit: Contact people through the directory, not through the message.
- **Module 2: The trusted request**: Attackers borrow authority and urgency because people want to help their manager and meet deadlines. You will be able to: Name the pressure tactics in an urgent request; Pause politely without refusing outright; Verify payments and calls through records you already hold.
    - Habit: Call back on a number you already have before you pay, reset or share.
- **Module 3: The message that fits your job**: The most convincing messages look like ordinary work: an invitation, a shared file, an account notice. You will be able to: Find the action a message is asking you to take; Read sender addresses and links without opening them; Recognise “safety signs” that prove nothing.
    - Habit: Go to the app or website yourself instead of using the link.
- **Module 4: Beyond the password**: Attackers no longer need your password if you approve a sign-in, a code, an app or a device for them. You will be able to: Explain what an approval actually grants; Respond to sign-in prompts you did not start; Recognise code, app-permission and device-linking tricks.
    - Habit: Approve only what you started and recognise.
- **Module 5: The helpful stranger**: Fake IT help, fake “verification” pages and fake renewal notices all try to get you to let them in. You will be able to: Check a support request before giving access; Stop when a web page asks you to run something; Tell genuine support from a fake offer.
    - Habit: No ticket you raised, no remote access.
- **Module 6: Stop the chain**: Real incidents rarely look like one obvious attack. They look like several small, separate events. You will be able to: Work as a team across operations, finance, management and IT; Separate facts from guesses; Report early, before you know everything.
    - Habit: Report early, even if you are not sure.
- **Module 7: Report and recover**: Mistakes happen. Fast, honest reporting limits the damage. You will be able to: Use your organisation’s reporting route; Write a report that helps the response team; Know what to do after different kinds of mistake.

## How the slides work

Most slides show everything at once: the evidence, numbered amber markers explaining it, and the slide’s **takeaway** beside or beneath the evidence (a short teal-ruled statement with its supporting actions). Ask the slide’s question before reading the answer aloud. Sixteen slides are **pause points** (marked below): the room votes or discusses first, then you click once to reveal the answer and its takeaway. Every module opens with a goal slide and ends with a takeaway slide and one habit. The “Key point” line below each slide is the summary used in these notes; on screen it appears as the takeaway, or as the slide’s own cards, table or feedback where those already say it.

## Delivery rhythm and language

- Show evidence without the answer. Ask for a decision and reasons. Reveal only after discussion.
- Accept “not enough evidence: verify” as a sound answer. Reward the route, not the label “phishing”.
- Explain why convenient options feel plausible. Do not shame wrong choices; feedback buttons say “Reconsider”, never “Wrong”.
- Include the genuine requests (SL26, SL36 card 3, SL57, SL73). Verification and authorisation are different checks.
- Use supportive reporting language: “Thank you for reporting. What did you see, and what did you do?” Never “Why did you click?”
- Do not say all attacks use AI, all MFA fails, MFA makes you safe, training prevents all phishing, or that most breaches begin with spear phishing.
- Government-sector participants can use their own approved examples in discussion. Do not invent sector-specific law, mandates or procedures.

## Deck controls

Right arrow or Page Down: next slide. Left arrow or Page Up: previous slide (presentation clickers send these). Home/End: first or last slide. M opens or closes the menu (top-right button), which holds the slide index grouped by module, presenter notes, sources, fullscreen, keyboard help, workshop information and “Reset this interaction”. F toggles fullscreen; ? opens keyboard help; Escape closes the open menu or panel. Only a slide counter stays on screen at the bottom-right. “Reset this interaction” appears only on slides with a vote or reveal and restores just that slide. Choices persist while you navigate and reset on reload. Nothing is stored or sent.

### M0: Opening baseline (10:00–10:20, 20 min)

#### SL01 · The request before 5 PM
10:00–10:01 · 1 min · cover · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Establish the fictional cast and baseline decision
- **Key screen text:** A familiar name. A payment deadline. / What would you check?
- **Run it:** Open the first message to show the full email.
- **Ask, then confirm:** No hidden answer. Let the room say what they would check before paying.
- **Notes:** Say Meranti is fictional. Farid is the central character of the opening; Aina, Mei and Ravi are introduced as they appear. Open the email when the room has read the headline. Do not disclose the outcome.
- Say: “Today we will practise handling requests involving information, account access and money. Some messages are genuine. We will focus on how to verify and what to do if we already acted.”
- Meranti, its people and messages are fictional and reusable across sectors. Documented cases later are labelled and cited. Nobody needs to share a personal incident.
- Farid is the central character of the opening. Aina and Mei appear later. Do not reveal the eventual fraud outcome.
- The cover carries an optional dusk-office backdrop at 15% opacity. It is decorative only; the headline and the email stay the two focal points.

#### SL02 · Today’s workshop
10:01–10:04 · 3 min · agenda · evidence: guidance

- **Objective:** What we will practise today, in what order, and how we will work together.
- **Say:** What we will practise today, in what order, and how we will work together.
- **Key point:** Today is about one habit: when a message asks for money, information or access, check it through a route you already trust.
- **Key screen text:** Spot when a message asks for money, information or access / Check requests through a route you already trust / Know what an approval, code or app permission really gives away / Report quickly and usefully, including your own mistakes
- **Notes:** Read the slide aloud briefly; it frames the module. No hidden content.
- Set expectations: everything is fictional, no wrong questions, nobody shares personal incidents, reporting is never blamed.

#### SL03 · A request that fits the job
10:04–10:06 · 2 min · email · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Inspect evidence without assuming trust
- **Say:** Farid gets an expected invoice email from a known supplier, but the bank details have changed.
- **Key point:** A correct sender address and a familiar conversation do not prove who is writing. A change to bank details always needs an independent check.
- **Key screen text:** What can this email actually prove?
- **Run it:** Expand sender and destination.
- **Ask, then confirm:** The email proves little: the sender and destination both use the expected fictional supplier domain, but that does not show who controls the mailbox or whether the bank change is genuine.
- **Notes:** Ask what changed and what must be verified. Use the prototype text.
- Let participants inspect the sender and the destination. This is intentionally a hard example involving possible account misuse, not an obvious typo.
- Ask: What changed? How would you verify it? No attachment opens.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL04 · Another familiar name appears
10:06–10:08 · 2 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Recognise pressure from an apparent manager
- **Say:** A chat using the manager’s name pushes Farid to pay quickly.
- **Key point:** A display name and urgency tell you nothing about who controls the account. Pressure to skip a check is a reason to slow down.
- **Key screen text:** Does this conversation give Farid enough confidence to pay?
- **Run it:** Reveal messages one by one; replay.
- **Ask, then confirm:** No. A display name and a deadline say little about who controls the account.
- **Notes:** Ask what changed in the evidence. A display name is insufficient.
- Reveal one message at a time. After each, ask whether the evidence supports making the bank change.
- Participants should feel comfortable keeping approval procedures even under pressure from an apparent manager.
- The desk photograph is an AI-generated illustration of Farid (fictional); no readable screen or chat content is shown. It illustrates the scene and is not evidence.
- The point for this scene is on the next slide, after the room has answered.

#### SL04B · What the two messages can prove
10:08–10:10 · 2 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** State what the email and the chat can and cannot prove
- **Say:** Neither message proves who is asking. The bank change still needs an independent check.
- **Key point:** A correct sender address, a familiar conversation, a display name and urgency do not prove who is writing. A change to bank details always needs an independent check, and pressure to skip it is a reason to slow down.
- **Key screen text:** A correct sender address and a familiar conversation do not prove who is writing. / A display name and urgency tell you nothing about who controls the account.
- **Run it:** Give the explanation after the room has answered both questions; then move to the decision.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Little. The email’s matching address and the chat’s display name show only what a sender chose to display; neither shows who controls the account or whether the bank change is genuine. Farid’s call to the number in the supplier record is the check that can.
- **Notes:** Explanation stage for scenes 01 and 02. Use the answers the room gave. Both points lead to the decision on the next slide.
- Explanation stage for scenes 01 and 02 (layout fix, 8 Oct 2026): the room answers both questions first, then this slide gives the two points. The desk photograph stays on the previous slide; no new scene.
- Keep the link to the decision: the next slide asks what Farid should do.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL05 · What should Farid do next?
10:10–10:14 · 4 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Choose independent verification
- **Say:** Your first decision of the day. Vote with a show of hands, then select the answer the room chose.
- **Key point:** Verify through a contact you already hold, such as the supplier record, then follow the normal approval process. Replying to the same email cannot verify anything.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** Choose an action. / What makes the verification route trustworthy?
- **Run it:** Vote before selecting.
- **Ask, then confirm:** C: call the supplier using existing records, then follow normal approval. B relies on the same possibly compromised channel; A leaves the change unverified.
- **Notes:** A genuine request would still need the same process.
- Baseline decision (see ASSESSMENT.md). Ask for a show of hands before selecting. Record reasoning, not names.
- Do not shame an incorrect choice. Discuss why it feels convenient. A genuine payment change would still need the same controls.
- **Choices (SL05):**
    - A. Pay using revised details: The bank change remains unverified. A familiar invoice and an apparent manager’s instruction do not verify the new bank account.
    - B. Reply to Nadia for confirmation: The same mailbox cannot provide an independent check. If someone controls the mailbox, they can also send the confirmation.
    - C. Call the supplier using existing records: This gives an independent verification route. Use the supplier’s established contact details, then follow the normal payment approval process. ← recommended
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL06 · The callback changes the picture
10:14–10:17 · 3 min · annotated · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Separate original clues from newly verified facts
- **Say:** Farid calls the supplier on the number already held in the finance system.
- **Key point:** Independent verification gives you facts the message never could. Hold the payment, keep the evidence and report.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** The supplier denies the change. / Ravi denies sending the chat. / Farid holds the payment and reports.
- **Run it:** Reveal findings.
- **Ask, then confirm:** The callback adds facts the messages could not provide: the supplier denies the change and Ravi denies the chat. Farid holds and reports.
- **Notes:** Do not imply participants should have guessed facts revealed only now. IT investigates account misuse.
- Reveal only after discussion. These are fictional facts disclosed now, not clues the audience could have spotted earlier.
- IT investigates how the identities were misused. Preserve evidence and use the organisation’s actual reporting channel.
- Source wording: the FBI IC3 page advises verifying through secondary channels. “Existing records” is this course’s practical form of that advice.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL07 · When the meeting looked convincing
10:17–10:20 · 3 min · case · evidence: documented

- **Objective:** Apply verification to a documented video fraud
- **Say:** A real case: a fabricated video meeting helped convince an employee to transfer about HK$200 million.
- **Key point:** Even a convincing meeting can be fabricated. A separate, authorised payment check is what stops the loss.
- **Key screen text:** Approximate reported loss: HK$200m / Email, prerecorded video and payment messages
- **Run it:** Ask which independent check could interrupt the sequence.
- **Ask, then confirm:** An independent, authorised transaction workflow, such as a call-back on a known number and a second approver, could interrupt the sequence regardless of how convincing the meeting looked.
- **Notes:** Preserve prerecorded/no-interaction detail. No victim screenshot or invented dialogue.
- Official account: Hong Kong Government LCQ9, 26 June 2024, describing an incident in January 2024. About HK$200 million; an email impersonating the CFO; a fabricated, prerecorded video conference with no interaction; transfers to five local bank accounts; later instructions by instant messaging.
- Do not describe this as proven real-time interactive AI. Do not name the company or invent dialogue.
- **Sources:** S9 Hong Kong Government LCQ9

#### SL09 · Impersonation and phishing
10:22–10:24 · 2 min · comparison · evidence: guidance

- **Objective:** Distinguish concepts
- **Say:** Three words we use all day.
- **Key point:** Impersonation borrows a trusted identity; phishing asks you to act; spear phishing aims at you specifically.
- **Key screen text:** Impersonation / Phishing / Spear phishing
- **Run it:** Define the three words; the overlap follows on the next slide.
- **Ask, then confirm:** The techniques can overlap.
- **Notes:** Keep terms plain. Definitions are course paraphrases.
- Definitions are course paraphrases in plain English. MITRE ATT&CK T1566 lists phishing sub-techniques (attachment, link, via service, voice) if participants ask for a taxonomy.
- Optional risk context for the trainer only: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR reports vulnerability exploitation as the leading initial access vector, at 31% of breaches analysed (incidents from 1 November 2024 to 31 October 2025). Do not say most attacks begin with spear phishing.
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams; S10 MITRE ATT&CK T1566

#### SL09B · One message can do all three
10:24–10:25 · 1 min · comparison · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Show how impersonation, spear phishing and phishing overlap in one attack
- **Say:** One fictional story in three steps. Which word describes each step?
- **Key point:** One message can do all three: borrow an identity, aim at you specifically and ask you to act.
- **Key screen text:** One story, three steps / Which word describes each step?
- **Run it:** Ask which concept describes each step.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Step 1 is impersonation; step 2 targets a particular group (spear phishing); step 3 asks for a harmful action (phishing). One incident can involve all three.
- **Notes:** Keep terms plain. Ask the room to name the concept for each step before you do.
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams; S10 MITRE ATT&CK T1566

#### SL10 · What can someone learn about Aina?
10:25–10:31 · 6 min · profile · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Identify public context used in persuasive messages
- **Say:** Everything on Aina’s public profile that a stranger could reuse.
- **Key point:** Public work details make a fake message feel expected. Knowing them does not prove the sender works with you.
- **Key screen text:** Job title / Project announcement / Supplier and colleague names
- **Run it:** Reveal public details; identify one that makes a message credible.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Job title, project, colleague and supplier names, and an event date can all make a message feel expected. None proves the sender works with Aina or has authority.
- **Notes:** Use only invented posts. Explain that public context can reduce suspicion without victim blame.
- Use only these invented posts. Public context reduces suspicion; that is a normal human reaction, not carelessness. Avoid victim blame.
- If asked: organisations can agree what staff share publicly about projects, but the course does not prescribe a social-media policy.
- **Sources:** S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks

#### SL11 · Two profiles with the same face
10:31–10:37 · 6 min · comparison · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Avoid judging authenticity from copied profile details
- **Say:** Two profiles with the same photo, name and posts. Can you tell which is real?
- **Key point:** You cannot tell from the screen. Photos, names, posts and follower counts can all be copied. Contact the person through the staff directory.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** Which details can be copied? / How would you contact Aina independently?
- **Run it:** Compare profiles; select verify rather than guessing.
- **Ask, then confirm:** C: contact Aina through the staff directory. Neither profile can be shown to be genuine from the screen.
- **Notes:** No score for guessing from account age or follower counts.
- Give no credit for guessing from account age, follower counts or handle style; these can be bought, built or copied.
- Which details can be copied? Photo, name, title, posts, handle style and even mutual connections.
- **Choices (SL11-pick):**
    - A. Profile A is the real Aina: The screen cannot tell you that. Names, photos and posts can all be copied.
    - B. Profile B is the real Aina: The screen cannot tell you that. Account age and followers can be faked too.
    - C. Contact Aina through the staff directory: Verify outside both profiles. Use the directory or a known number. ← recommended
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams

#### SL12 · A genuine account, an unusual request
10:37–10:39 · 2 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Understand compromised account risk
- **Say:** A real colleague’s account asks Aina for the full staff contact list.
- **Key point:** A genuine account can still be used by someone else, and even a genuine request needs permission.
- **Key screen text:** The account may be real. / The request still needs authorisation.
- **Run it:** Reveal request, then ask how to verify need and permitted disclosure.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Follow data-sharing rules and independently verify the purpose.
- **Notes:** Let the room read the chat. Ask what the request would disclose before showing the findings.
- Even if Siti really sent it, a full staff contact list may be more than the task needs.
- Ask what the request would disclose before moving on; the findings and the copied/taken-over diagram are on the next slide.
- **Sources:** S8 Joint Scattered Spider advisory; S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks

#### SL12B · Two checks before sharing the list
10:39–10:41 · 2 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Separate verifying the purpose from permitted disclosure, and account takeover from profile cloning
- **Say:** What Aina does with the request, and why a known account is not proof of who is typing.
- **Key point:** Verify the purpose separately and share only what is needed, through the approved route.
- **Key screen text:** Verify the purpose separately / Follow data-sharing rules / Copied profile or taken-over account
- **Run it:** Ask how to verify the need and what may be disclosed; then explain the diagram.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Verify the purpose through the directory and share only what the event needs through the approved route. The account may genuinely be Siti’s and still be controlled by someone else.
- **Notes:** Distinguish account compromise from profile cloning. Both can send the same message, so both need an independent check.
- Distinguish compromise (someone controls the genuine account) from cloning (a separate copy). The response differs: see SL15.
- The diagram replaces the earlier hint: cloning copies a profile (a separate account), compromise means someone else controls the real account. Both can send this message, so both need an independent check.
- **Sources:** S8 Joint Scattered Spider advisory; S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks

#### SL13 · The support page that found you
10:41–10:46 · 5 min · browser · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Recognise brand impersonation
- **Say:** Aina complains publicly about a login problem and “support” replies within minutes.
- **Key point:** If support found you, do not use it. Start from the app, your saved bookmark or your IT helpdesk.
- **Key screen text:** An unsolicited support contact offers to fix an account issue.
- **Run it:** Inspect claimed identity and route to known support.
- **Ask, then confirm:** The support contact found Aina, not the other way round. Start support from the known service: saved bookmark, installed app or the IT helpdesk.
- **Notes:** Do not suggest every advert is malicious.
- Do not suggest every advert or reply is malicious. The safe habit is choosing the route yourself.
- Never send a code you receive to anyone. The fictional brand CloudDocs and all addresses use reserved .example names.
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams; S6 FTC impersonation scams analysis

#### SL14 · A collaboration that sounds relevant
10:46–10:53 · 7 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Reassess a sensitive action after a normal conversation
- **Say:** A friendly professional contact builds trust, then asks for a sign-in and internal documents.
- **Key point:** Re-check whenever a conversation reaches money, access or information, however friendly it has been.
- **Key screen text:** A normal conversation can lead to an unexpected request.
- **Run it:** Reveal benign opener then sensitive follow-up.
- **Ask, then confirm:** At message 2 (sign in with a work account) and message 3 (internal documents). The earlier friendly exchange does not authorise either.
- **Notes:** Pair exercise: identify the point requiring verification. Keep business names fictional.
- Pair exercise: three minutes. Each pair names the point requiring verification and the route they would use.
- Riverside Partners and Daniel are fictional.
- **Sources:** S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks

#### SL15 · Someone is using your name
10:53–10:56 · 3 min · response · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Respond to cloning versus takeover
- **Say:** What to do when someone pretends to be you, and how that differs from someone taking over your account.
- **Key point:** Preserve the evidence, then report and warn affected contacts through a trusted channel.
- **Key screen text:** Preserve the profile details. / Report and warn affected contacts through a trusted channel. / Use official account recovery if the genuine account is compromised.
- **Run it:** Walk through the three responses; the sorting table follows.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Preserve, report and warn. The sorting of actions by situation follows on the next slide.
- **Notes:** Internal security/communications owns work-related coordination. Avoid promising platform takedown times.
- Internal security or communications owns coordination for work-related impersonation. Do not promise platform takedown times.
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams

#### SL15B · Copied profile or taken-over account?
10:56–10:58 · 2 min · response · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Match each response action to cloning or takeover
- **Say:** Which action fits which situation.
- **Key point:** A copied profile needs a platform report; a taken-over account needs official recovery. Both need you to warn contacts through a trusted channel.
- **Key screen text:** Which action fits which situation? / Password changes alone do not remove a copied profile.
- **Run it:** Sort cloning and takeover response cards.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Report the copy: copied profile. Official recovery: takeover. Warn contacts through a trusted channel: both. Preserving details applies to both.
- **Notes:** A password change secures the genuine account but does nothing about a separate copied profile. Avoid promising platform takedown times.
- A password change secures the genuine account but does nothing about a separate copied profile.
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams

#### SL16 · Verify before you classify
10:58–11:03 · 5 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Choose a next action with uncertain identity
- **Say:** A familiar profile asks Farid for a supplier contract.
- **Key point:** Verify through the staff directory, then check the contract may be shared that way.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** A profile looks familiar, but the request is new.
- **Run it:** Choose: trust photo, continue in chat, verify through directory.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Contact Aina through the staff directory, then check whether the contract may be shared and how.
- **Notes:** Ask learners to justify the route, not only the classification.
- Ask learners to justify the route, not only the label (“it’s phishing”). “Not enough evidence: verify” is a sound answer.
- **Choices (SL16):**
    - A. Trust the photo: Profile details can be copied. A photo, name and job title are exactly what a copied profile reproduces.
    - B. Ask in the same chat: The person controlling that chat can answer. If someone else controls the chat, they will simply say yes.
    - C. Contact through the staff directory: Verify independently and check sharing permissions. Even if Aina really sent it, confirm she needs the contract and that sharing it this way is allowed. ← recommended
- **Sources:** S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams; S20 NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1

#### SL20 · An urgent request from the manager
11:17–11:21 · 4 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Notice authority pressure
- **Say:** “Ravi” asks Farid to pay a new supplier now and approve it later.

- **Run it:** Reveal request and secrecy instruction.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Confirm through established channels (Ravi’s directory number) and use the normal purchasing approval, even under deadline.
- **Notes:** Connect to opening without replaying its six slides.
- Connect to the opening without replaying it: the pattern is authority plus urgency plus a process exception.
- Managers in the room: say explicitly that you will support staff who pause to verify.
- The desk photograph is an AI-generated illustration of Farid (fictional) reading the request; no readable screen or chat content is shown.

#### SL21 · What the pressure asks you to skip
11:21–11:27 · 6 min · annotated · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Identify process bypass
- **Say:** The three pressure tactics hidden in one short message.
- **Key point:** Urgency, secrecy and “I’ll approve it later” all try to remove a check. The risk is the exception, even if the sender is genuine.
- **Key screen text:** Urgency / Secrecy / An exception to normal approval
- **Run it:** Identify the business check being bypassed.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Urgency, secrecy and an exception to normal approval. The risk is the exception itself, even if the sender is genuine.
- **Notes:** Discuss authority, fear and helpfulness without stereotyping victims.
- Discuss authority, fear and helpfulness as normal reactions. Do not stereotype who falls for this.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL22 · A polite way to pause
11:27–11:33 · 6 min · roleplay · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Practise a usable response
- **Say:** Practise saying “not yet” politely to someone senior.
- **Key point:** Name the route and the next step: “I’ll call you back on your directory number, then raise it for approval.”
- **Key screen text:** “I can help once I confirm through our normal approval process.”
- **Run it:** Two-minute roleplay, swap, debrief.
- **Ask, then confirm:** A strong response is polite, names a specific route (directory number, approval system) and states the next step and rough time.
- **Notes:** Make room for cultural/authority concerns. Managers should support this behaviour.
- Two minutes per round, then swap. Make room for cultural and hierarchy concerns: what makes challenging a senior person hard here?
- Do not reward refusing everything without escalation. Managers should model welcoming the pause.
- **Sources:** S20 NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1

#### SL23 · The voice on the phone
11:33–11:37 · 4 min · voice · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** A caller knows Aina’s name and manager, and asks her to read out a code.

- Read the script aloud; no recording or voice cloning of real people is used.
- The joint Scattered Spider advisory (updated 29 July 2025) describes helpdesk impersonation and phone-based social engineering. Our recheck could not retrieve that page on 2 October 2026; the description rests on the earlier research review.
- The desk photograph is an AI-generated illustration of Aina (fictional) taking the call; the caller is deliberately not shown and no real person is depicted.
- **Sources:** S8 Joint Scattered Spider advisory

#### SL23B · What proves who is calling?
11:37–11:39 · 2 min · voice · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** What to do when a caller asks for a reset or a code.

#### SL24 · A face or voice cannot approve a payment
11:39–11:46 · 7 min · case · evidence: guidance

- **Ask, then confirm:** Spotting glitches is unreliable as the only defence; an independent, authorised transaction process works whether or not the media is fake.

- Do not claim all synthetic media is detectable, or that all video calls are unsafe.

#### SL25 · Which number will you call?
11:46–11:53 · 7 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Choose existing contact records
- **Say:** A bank-change email gives Farid a new number to call.
- **Key point:** Call the number already in your records, never one supplied with the change.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** The email includes a new phone number to confirm new bank details.
- **Run it:** Choose callback destination, explain rationale.
- **Ask, then confirm:** B: the existing vendor record. A number supplied with the change comes from the same unverified request.
- **Notes:** The genuine vendor may have a new number too; update records through approved procedure.
- The genuine vendor may really have a new number too. Then update the record through the approved procedure before relying on it.
- Option C: pausing is right, but the payment owner and security need to know.
- **Choices (SL25):**
    - A. New number in the email: It comes from the same unverified request. Whoever sent the change also controls that number.
    - B. Existing vendor record: Use the established contact and required approval. If Maju’s number has genuinely changed, update the record through the approved procedure first. ← recommended
    - C. Wait without telling anyone: Hold the action and notify the appropriate owner. Pausing is right, but the payment owner and security need to know.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise; S5 FTC Business Impersonator Scams

#### SL26 · Keep the process when the request is genuine
11:53–11:58 · 5 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Avoid labelling all sensitive requests as fraud
- **Say:** The supplier confirms the bank change is real. Can Farid pay now?
- **Key point:** Verification checks who is asking. Authorisation decides whether it may happen. A genuine change still goes through approval.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** A verified vendor really has changed banks.
- **Run it:** Ask whether verification alone permits payment.
- **Ask, then confirm:** B: complete the approved bank-change and payment process. Verification (who) and authorisation (whether) serve different purposes.
- **Notes:** Explicit legitimate example. Verification and authorisation serve different purposes.
- This is an explicit legitimate example. Learners should not leave thinking every bank change is fraud.
- **Choices (SL26):**
    - A. Pay immediately after the call: Identity verification does not replace payment authorisation. The call answers who is asking. It does not replace the approval step.
    - B. Complete the approved bank-change and payment process: Proceed only after verification, records and approvals are complete. A genuine change still follows the bank-change and payment controls. ← recommended
    - C. Treat every bank change as fraud: A verified legitimate change can proceed through the proper process. Treating genuine requests as fraud damages trust and still skips the process.
- **Sources:** S7 FBI IC3 Business Email Compromise

#### SL29 · A message that fits your work
12:02–12:07 · 5 min · email · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Identify the requested action
- **Say:** Three ordinary work messages, each asking for a different risky action.
- **Key point:** Look for the action: sign in, share data, open a file. Then verify outside the message. Any of these could be genuine.

- **Run it:** Ask which action creates risk.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Calendar: sign in from a link. HR: disclose personal and bank data. Shared file: open, possibly then sign in. Any could be genuine; each needs the three questions.

#### SL30 · The sender behind the display name
12:07–12:13 · 6 min · email · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** What the full sender address reveals behind the display name.

- **Ask, then confirm:** The display name says Ravi; the address and reply-to are a free-mail account, not his directory address. That mismatch is a clue. A matching address would still need the request verified.

- In notes only, not as a protocol lecture: display names are free text; lookalike domains imitate real ones; a compromised mailbox sends from the real address.
- **Sources:** S10 MITRE ATT&CK T1566

#### SL31 · The destination behind the label
12:13–12:18 · 5 min · browser · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** Who really controls this link? Vote, then see how to read it.

#### SL42 · Access can be granted without sharing a password
14:18–14:23 · 5 min · comparison · evidence: guidance

- **Say:** Four ways to give someone access without sharing a password.

#### SL43 · The login session an attacker can reuse
14:23–14:29 · 6 min · browser · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Understand session theft at a high level
- **Say:** How a fake sign-in page can capture a working login, even with MFA.
- **Key point:** Sign in from your bookmark or app, not from a link. Phishing-resistant MFA, such as security keys and passkeys, blocks this relay.
- **Key screen text:** A deceptive sign-in flow may capture a usable session.
- **Run it:** Reveal the access consequence.
- **Ask, then confirm:** The relay obtains a valid session and can reuse it while that session remains valid and the service’s controls allow it, often without the password or another prompt.
- **Notes:** Describe AiTM conceptually. No proxy code or live capture. Do not say MFA is pointless.
- Adversary-in-the-middle, described conceptually. No proxy code or live capture is shown, and there are no credential fields.
- Do not say MFA is pointless. CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO/WebAuthn, PKI) because it is bound to the genuine site. The CISA fact sheet is dated October 2022.
- The relay diagram replaces the three mock screens (a lookalike page with no fields, the real MFA prompt, “someone else’s browser”). The page passes what Aina types to the real service; the real service asks her to approve; the relay keeps the session the service issues.
- Whether and for how long a captured session works depends on its validity and the service’s session controls (Microsoft, 29 May 2025). A new password or MFA prompt may not be requested for that access, but this is not guaranteed in every service.
- **Sources:** S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks; S13 CISA phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet

- **Ask, then confirm:** A: deny each prompt and report it.

- MFA remains useful. Number matching reduces some risks but does not legitimise a request you did not start.
- Repeated prompts may mean the password is known: IT can investigate and reset.

#### SL45B · Whose device the code would sign in
14:38–14:42 · 4 min · browser · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** Where the code came from, and what authorising it would do.

- **Run it:** Reveal who initiated the request.

- No real device code is shown. The service address being genuine does not validate the request.
- Device-code phishing works through the legitimate sign-in flow: Aina must enter the code on the real page, authenticate if asked and authorise the request; entering the code alone is not described as an unconditional grant (Microsoft, 6 April 2026).

#### SL47 · Linking another device
14:48–14:51 · 3 min · qr · evidence: fictional

#### SL47B · Joining a group or linking a device?
14:51–14:53 · 2 min · qr · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** Joining adds you to one conversation. Linking gives another device your account.

- **Key screen text:** Joining a group / Linking a device / Link only devices you own and set up yourself
- **Run it:** Reveal difference between joining a group and linking a device.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Joining a group adds you to a conversation; linking a device gives that device ongoing access to your account. This QR would link a device.

#### SL48 · A defence that stopped the attempted access
14:53–14:58 · 5 min · case · evidence: documented

- **Objective:** Understand layered controls
- **Say:** A real case where staff entered passwords but security keys stopped the attack.
- **Key point:** Strong controls and quick reporting work together. Some MFA types resist phishing much better than others.
- **Key screen text:** Cloudflare reported three credential submissions. / Hardware-key requirements prevented the attempted access.
- **Run it:** Compare credential exposure with prevented access.
- **Ask, then confirm:** Credentials were exposed, but access was prevented because sign-in required hardware security keys. Layered controls and prompt response worked together.
- **Notes:** Historical positive case. Do not promise keys prevent consent or payment fraud.
- Cloudflare’s first-party post (9 August 2022) describes the 20 July 2022 SMS campaign: three employees entered credentials; FIDO2 keys prevented the logins.
- Historical positive case. Do not blame staff. Do not promise keys prevent consent abuse or payment fraud.
- **Sources:** S14 Cloudflare phishing incident disclosure; S13 CISA phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet

#### SL49 · What does this approval grant?
14:58–15:03 · 5 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Distinguish authentication from business authority
- **Say:** A trusted service asks you to approve an unfamiliar session.
- **Key point:** Check where the request came from through a route you know. If you did not start it, deny it and report it.
- **Pause point:** let the room vote or discuss before clicking.
- **Key screen text:** A trusted service asks you to approve an unfamiliar session.
- **Run it:** Identify grant and independent route.
- **Ask, then confirm:** B: check the initiating session or app through the known route.
- **Notes:** Ask for learner explanation rather than technical vocabulary.
- Ask for the learner’s explanation in plain words rather than technical vocabulary.
- **Choices (SL49):**
    - A. Approve because the service is genuine: The request may authorise someone else’s session or an unwanted app. A real service can still sign in someone else’s device or app.
    - B. Check the initiating session or app through the known route: Verify what access is granted and why before acting. If you did not start it, deny or cancel and report it. ← recommended
    - C. Disable MFA to avoid prompts: MFA remains useful; report suspicious requests rather than disabling it. MFA still blocks many attacks. Report unexpected prompts instead.
- **Sources:** S11 Microsoft evolving identity attacks; S12 Microsoft AI-enabled device-code campaign

#### SL52 · Mei offers help in chat
15:07–15:11 · 4 min · chat · evidence: fictional

- **Say:** Someone using Mei’s name and photo offers to fix a problem Aina never reported.

#### SL53 · Remote access changes the stakes
15:11–15:17 · 6 min · decision · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Require verified support authorisation
- **Say:** A remote-control request appears on Aina’s screen.
- **Key point:** No ticket, no session. Check with the helpdesk first, and never send a login code to prove anything.

- **Choices (SL53):**
    - A. Accept control because the tool is well known: A legitimate tool can still enable unauthorised access. A legitimate tool can give a stranger full control.
    - B. Verify the ticket through the established helpdesk: Check support identity, purpose and authorised access before proceeding. A genuine technician can wait while you check. ← recommended
    - C. Send a login code to prove the account: Do not disclose codes to an unsolicited caller. IT will never need you to read out a code.
- **Sources:** S8 Joint Scattered Spider advisory; S15 Microsoft threats targeting Teams

#### SL54B · What that step would actually do
15:20–15:22 · 2 min · browser · evidence: fictional

- **Objective:** Explain what pasting a page’s text into a system tool can cause, and what to do
- **Say:** What pasting the page’s text into a system tool could do, and what to do instead.
- **Key point:** Stop, close the page and contact IT. If anything already ran, report it immediately.
- **Key screen text:** Pasted text can execute instructions / Possible harm: data theft or remote control / Stop. Contact IT using your known route.
- **Run it:** Reveal the request to run a supposed verification action.
- **Ask, then confirm:** It could run whatever instructions the page supplied on the computer. What follows, from nothing to data theft or remote control, depends on what ran and what was blocked. Stop, close the page and contact approved support; if anything already ran, report immediately.
- **Notes:** Outcomes are possible, not guaranteed: they depend on what ran and what was blocked.
- ClickFix (Microsoft, 21 August 2025): fake verification or ‘fix’ steps lead people to paste and run commands themselves.
- The consequence diagram replaces the earlier hint: typing or pasting instructions from a web page into a system tool can run software on your computer; that is the attack (Microsoft ClickFix analysis, 21 August 2025). The outcomes shown are possible, not guaranteed: they depend on what ran and which protections blocked it.
- **Sources:** S16 Microsoft ClickFix analysis

#### SL55 · A browser problem becomes a repair request
15:22–15:28 · 6 min · case · evidence: documented

- **Say:** A documented technique: a fake extension breaks your browser, then offers a harmful “fix”.

- **Run it:** Reveal installation, delay, problem, repair pretext.

- The ‘delay’ stage is from the package’s research summary; our 2 October recheck excerpt confirmed the impersonation, crash and repair prompt. Do not invent losses or reproduce extension code.
- **Sources:** S17 Microsoft CrashFix

#### SL57 · Which support request can you proceed with?

## Answer keys

### SL36 four-request activity

The card set follows `slides.json`. `08-facilitator/EXERCISES_AND_ANSWER_KEYS.md` lists an HR card instead of the IT notice; the genuine HR request is kept for SL73 so the post-check uses a fresh situation.

| Card | Hidden fact | Preferred action | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Vendor | Genuine change, not yet approved | Verify first: established contact, then the change/approval process | Legitimate sensitive changes still need controls |
| 2 Colleague | Genuine account, someone else using it | Verify first through the directory; report concerning activity | A known account can carry an attacker’s request |
| 3 IT notice | Genuine notice inside the portal Aina opened herself | Proceed under normal policy | Reached through a known route; asks for nothing sensitive |
| 4 Manager | Impersonated urgent exception | Hold and report; verify through the directory; notify owner and security | A deadline and display name cannot remove an approval |

Reveal only the visible request first. Groups explain what facts they need to proceed. Do not report a verified legitimate request as malicious only because it is sensitive.

### M4 identity approvals

| Prompt | What it could grant | Safer action |
|---|---|---|
| Unexpected MFA | Access for a sign-in attempt | Deny and report; never disable MFA |
| Supplied device code | Access for the device or session that generated it | Do not enter unsolicited codes; check purpose |
| App permissions | Access to the listed data and functions | Use the approved app process |
| Linking QR | Ongoing access by a linked device | Link only recognised devices you started |

### M5 support verification

Unsolicited support: contact the established helpdesk or ticket independently before any remote access. Confirmed ticket: follow the normal authorised support procedure and data rules. Do not teach blanket rejection of support.

## Tabletop (M6, 35 minutes)

Roles per table: Operations (Aina), Finance (Farid), Manager (Ravi), IT support (Mei). Setup 3 min; cards T1–T4 (6, 7, 7, 7 min); debrief 5 min. Required group output: known facts; unverified claims; next safe actions with owners; a short report. Record hypotheses separately; do not conclude one event caused another without evidence.

Rubric, 0–2 each (course rubric, not a NIST certification score): 1) identifies the sensitive action and its consequence; 2) chooses independent established verification; 3) maintains approval and data-sharing requirements; 4) reports promptly with useful facts and an owner; 5) avoids further unsafe interaction and preserves evidence. 0 = absent or unsafe; 1 = partly correct, missing route or owner; 2 = specific and appropriate. Give group feedback without names or rankings.

## Response after a mistake

| Situation | Employee action | Responsible follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| Suspicious message, no interaction | Use the approved report action; keep the original | Security assesses related activity |
| Opened a link | Stop interacting; report exactly what happened | Security checks for download, access or execution |
| Entered credentials or approved a session | Report immediately through a trusted route | IT/security revoke sessions and tokens; reset credentials as appropriate |
| Granted app permissions or linked a device | Report the app/device and time | IT removes unauthorised grants/devices and investigates |
| Ran software or allowed control | Stop; follow the incident procedure; contact IT from another device if needed | Contain the device, preserve evidence; avoid unplanned wipe or restart |
| Transferred money | Tell finance and security; contact the bank through its established channel immediately | Attempt recovery; coordinate records and external reports |
| Found a copied profile | Preserve link, handle, screenshots and times; notify | Communications/security coordinate platform report and contact warning |

A useful report: time and time zone, channel, claimed sender, action taken, device, original evidence if available, and any uncertainty. Never include passwords, one-time codes or tokens. This table is a course synthesis (sources S7, S12, S20), not verbatim official instructions. MyCERT’s Cyber999 (S19) is an external Malaysian route and does not replace the internal procedure.

## Assessment and follow-up

SL05 is the baseline decision; SL73 is a parallel post-check with a different surface (HR data). Score whether the learner identifies the action, uses an independent route, keeps authorisation, and reports or recovers appropriately. No pass mark is imposed and no identifiable scores are collected. An optional 30-day refresher (`09-participant/REFRESHER_30_DAYS.md`) is a proposed programme step; nothing is scheduled or sent by this build. If an authorised simulation is used later, interpret results with the NIST Phish Scale (S18); clicks and opens do not prove credential exposure or negligence.
